dialogues.title: Dialogue 2
dialogues.setting: Mr. Ho hasn't seen Mr. Cheung for a long while. They meet by chance.

lines.speaker: Ho
lines.zh: 张先生，好耐冇见。你好吗？你而家喺边度住呀？
lines.jp: zoeng1 sin1 saang1, hou2 noi6 mou5 gin3. nei5 hou2 maa3? nei5 ji4 gaa1 hai2 bin1 dou6 zyu6 aa3?
lines.en: Mr. Cheung, long time no see. How are you? Where do you live now?

lines.speaker: Cheung
lines.zh: 我而家住喺香港花园道二十八号三楼。
lines.jp: ngo5 ji4 gaa1 zyu6 hai2 hoeng1 gong2 faa1 jyun4 dou6 ji6 sap6 baat3 hou6 saam1 lau2

lines.speaker: Ho
lines.jp: faa1 jyun4 dou6 hou2 m4 hou2 zyu6 aa3?

lines.speaker: Cheung
lines.zh: 好住。花园道有好多巴士同的士搭。何先生，你住喺边处呀？

lines.speaker: Ho
lines.zh: 我仲住喺咖啡街七十三号地下。你有时间请黎坐喇。
lines.jp: ngo5 zung6 zyu6 hai2 gaa3 fe1 gaai1 cat1 sap6 saam1 hou6 dei6 haa2. nei5 jau5 si4 gaan3 cing2 lai4 co5 laa1

lines.speaker: Cheung
lines.zh: 你有心。你间屋有车房吗？
lines.jp: nei5 jau5 sam1. nei5 gaan1 nguk1 jau5 ce1 fong4 maa3?

lines.speaker: Ho
lines.zh: 我唔係住一间屋，我住一层楼啫。呢层楼唔係几大，冇车房嘅。

lines.speaker: Cheung
lines.zh: 好，有时间我黎探你，再见。
lines.jp: hou2, jau5 si4 gaan3 ngo5 lai4 taam3 nei5, zoi3 gin3

grammar.title: Where?
grammar.summary: bin1 dou6? and bin1 cyu3 both mean where? and work to the same rule as bin1 go3 who? and mat1 je5 what?
grammar.body:
bin1 dou6? Where? Works to the same rule as bin1 go3 who? And mat1 je5 what?
bin1 dou6? And bin1 cyu3 both mean Where? And you can use whichever of them you prefer

grammar.title: Faan1 To return
grammar.summary: faan1 means to return; faan1 heoi3 is to go back, and faan1 also means to go where one usually goes.
grammar.body:
Faan1 means to return. It combines easily with heoi3 to go as meaning to faan1 heoi3 go back, that is to return in a direction away from me the speaker.
Faan1 also means to go where one usually goes.

examples.jp: nei5 faan1 heoi3 m4 faan1 heoi3 aa3
nei5 faan1 m4 faan1 heoi3 aa3
examples.en: Are you going back? (more commonly shortened form)

examples.jp: wong4 siu2 ze2 faan1 nguk1 kei5

grammar.title: Why?
grammar.summary: zou6 mat1 je5 literally means to do what? but has come to mean why?; it can be positioned quite freely in the sentence.
grammar.body:
zou6 mat1 je5 literally means to do what? But it has come to mean why?
It can be positioned quite freely in the sentence without any change of meaning: all the following examples mean Why must you sell your car?

examples.jp: nei5 zou6 mat1 je5 jiu3 maai6 ce1 aa3?
examples.en: Why must you sell your car?

examples.jp: zou6 mat1 je5 nei5 jiu3 maai6 ce1 aa3?
examples.en: Why must you sell your car?

examples.jp: nei5 jiu3 maai6 ce1 zou6 mat1 je5 aa3?
examples.en: Why must you sell your car?

grammar.title: Yes and No
grammar.summary: There are no words for yes and no; answer with the positive or negative form of the verb, or with hai6 / m4 hai6 when the verb is not the focus.
grammar.body:
There are no words for yes and no in Cantonese.
You should use the positive or negative form of the appropriate verb, in answer to a question.
If it is not the verb itself which is the focus of the question, it is useful to use hai6 it is the case or m4 hai6 it is not the case, as in the dialogue.
hai6 and m4 hai6 come as close to yes and no as Cantonese gets.

examples.jp: nei5 heoi3 m4 heoi3 zung1 gwok3 aa3?

grammar.title: The adverb jat1 cai4 "together"
grammar.summary: jat1 cai4 together is an adverb and, like almost all adverbs, comes in front of the verb.
grammar.body: jat1 cai4 together, all together is an adverb and like almost all adverbs it comes in front of the verb in the sentence.

grammar.title: That's right, isn't it?
grammar.summary: aa4 comes at the end of a sentence to ask for confirmation that what you have said is correct.
grammar.body: The word aa4 comes at the end of a sentence to ask for confirmation that what you have said is correct.

examples.jp: nei5 hai6 zoeng1 sin1 saang1 aa4?

examples.en: I take it you're going to England, right?

grammar.title: That's how the case stands now
grammar.summary: laak3 comes at the end of the sentence to state the current position, often implying that things have changed.
grammar.body:
Laak3 comes at the end of the sentence to state what the current position is.
Naturally enough that means that often there has been some change before that position has been arrived at.

examples.jp: keoi5 m4 soeng2 maai5 ce1 laak3
examples.en: He doesn't want to buy a car anymore

grammar.title: Possession and existence: jau5
grammar.summary: jau5 to have serves as a main verb and as an auxiliary. Its negative is not m4 jau5 but a separate verb, mou5 not to have.
grammar.body:
The verb jau5 serves both as a main verb (I have a question) and as an auxiliary (have you sent the letter?).
The verb jau5 to have is an oddity. It is not made negative with m4: instead the negative of jau5 is another verb, mou5 not to have.

examples.jp: ngo5 jau5 jat1 go3 zai2 jat1 go3 neoi2
examples.en: I have a son and a daughter

examples.jp: nei5 hai6 m4 hai6 jing1 gwok3 jan4 aa3?
nei5 jau5 mou5 jing1 gwok3 ce1 aa3?
examples.en: A: Have you got an English car?
B: I haven't got a car

examples.jp: ngo5 dei6 mou5 sai3 lou6 zai2

grammar.title: The verb jau5: question form
grammar.summary: The question form puts jau5 and mou5 together as jau5 mou5 (not *jau5 m4 jau5).
grammar.body: The question form is composed by putting jau5 'have' and mou5 'not have' together as jau5 mou5 (not *jau5 m4 jau5).

examples.jp: nei5 jau5 mou5 man6 tai4 aa3?
ngo5 dei6 jau5 mou5 si4 gaan3 aa3?
keoi5 dei6 jau5 mou5 cin2 aa3?

grammar.title: Existential jau5
grammar.summary: jau5 can also mean there is, mou5 there is not, and jau5 mou5 is there…?. The sentence simply begins with the place expression; a verb can be added to show what is to be done with the item introduced.
grammar.body:
jau5 can also mean 'there is'. Similarly, mou5 can mean 'there is not' and jau5 mou5 'Is there…?'
No preposition is needed: the sentence simply begins with the place expression.
jau5 in this sense also serves to introduce an indefinite noun phrase.
A verb can be added to show what is to be done with the item introduced by jau5/mou5.

examples.jp: hoeng1 gong2 jau5 hou2 do1 dik1 si2
examples.en: There are lots of taxis in Hong Kong
examples.lit: Hong Kong have very many taxis

examples.jp: toi2 soeng6 min6 jau5 gei2 zek3 dip2
examples.en: There are a few plates on the table
examples.lit: Table on-top have a few plates

examples.en: A person is looking for you

examples.jp: jau5 gei2 go3 hok6 saang1 hou2 nau1
jau5 hou2 do1 haak3 jan4 lai4 zo2
ngo5 gam1 jat6 jau5 gung1 fo3 zou6
examples.en: I have homework to do today
examples.lit: I today have homework to do

examples.en: There are no clothes to buy here
examples.lit: Here have no clothes to buy

examples.jp: jap6 bin6 jau5 mou5 je5 sik6 aa3?
examples.en: Is there anything to eat inside?
examples.lit: Inside have or have not anything to eat

grammar.title: jau5 as auxiliary
grammar.summary: jau5 also serves as an auxiliary, but normally only in the negative form mou5 and in questions as jau5 mou5.
grammar.body: jau5 also serves as an auxiliary but normally only in the negative form mou5 and in questions as jau5 mou5.

examples.jp: keoi5 gam1 jat6 mou5 faan1 gung1
examples.en: He hasn't been to work today

examples.jp: ngo5 mou5 zou6 gwo3 sin1 saang1
keoi5 dei6 jau5 mou5 bun1 nguk1 aa3?
nei5 jau5 mou5 hok6 gwo3 pou2 tung1 waa2 aa3?

grammar.title: Adjectives formed with jau5
grammar.summary: jau5 and mou5 can be added to nouns to form adjectives.
grammar.body: Jau5 and mou5 can also be added to nouns to form adjectives.

grammar.title: From the general to the particular
grammar.summary: Chinese gives addresses (and, later, dates and times) from the general to the particular, from the large to the small: the opposite of English.
grammar.body:
When Mr. Cheung gives his address in the dialogue, you will see that he gives it in the order Hong Kong, Garden Road, No. 28, 3rd floor - i.e. in the opposite way to English.
Chinese always prefers to work from the general to the particular, from the large to the small.
We shall see later that it is the same with dates and times, so that the Chinese would translate 3:18p.m. on 17 May 2021 in the order 2021, May 17 p.m. 3:18.

examples.jp: hoeng1 gong2 faa1 jyun4 dou6 ji6 sap6 baat3 hou6 saam1 lau2
examples.zh: 香港花园道二十八号三楼
examples.en: Hong Kong, Garden Road, No. 28, 3rd floor

grammar.title: ze1
grammar.summary: ze1/zek1 is tacked on to the end of a sentence to give the meaning only, that's all.
grammar.body: ze1/zek1 is a very useful little word which is tacked on to the end of sentence to give the meaning only, that's all.

examples.jp: keoi5 jau5 jat1 zi1 bat1 ze1

grammar.title: Not very
grammar.summary: The verb hai6 is slipped into the not very construction: m4 hai6 gei2 … / m4 hai6 hou2 ….
grammar.body: You will need to remember that the verb hai6 is slipped into this not very construction.

examples.jp: m4 hai6 gei2 daai6/m4 hai6 hou2 daai6
ni1 cang4 lau2 m4 hai6 gei2 gwai3
examples.en: This flat is not very expensive

examples.jp: wong4 siu2 ze2 m4 hai6 hou2 leng3
examples.en: Miss Wong is not very pretty

grammar.title: Emphatic hai6 and ge3
grammar.summary: hai6 can serve to emphasize the following word(s), especially with the particle ge3 at the end of the sentence.
grammar.body: Hai6 can serve to emphasize the following word(s), especially with the particle ge3 at the end of the sentence.

examples.en: It was you who helped me (emphasizing the subject nei5)

examples.jp: ni1 bun2 syu1 hai6 bin1 go3 ge3?
examples.en: Who was it that gave (us) this book? (emphasizing the subject bin1 go3)

examples.jp: fung1 seon3 hai6 gam1 jat6 gei3 dou3 ge3
examples.en: It was today the letter arrived (emphasizing the adverb gam1 jat6)

grammar.title: A recap: Final particles
grammar.summary: Final particles are words added to the end of the sentence to round it off or give an extra meaning; a reminder of those learned so far.
grammar.body:
Words that are added to the end of the sentence to round it off or to give an extra meaning. They are usually called final particles and they are used a great deal in everyday speech. Here's a reminder of those you already know.
maa3 - a spoken question mark. It makes a statement into a question.
ne1? - the shortcut question word which asks follow-up questions.
aa3? - the final particle which is added to sentences which already contain positive-negative-type questions or question words like mat1 je5
gaa3? - the particle made when ge3 is followed by aa3?
aa4? - the question word which expects the listeners to be in agreement: that's right, isn't it?
laak3 - the word which shows that things were different before but this is how the situation stands now.
ze1/zek1 - only, that's all
laa1 - the word you use when you are trying to urge someone to do something for you or to persuade someone to agree with you.
ge3 - makes a statement more emphatic: That's the way it is!

examples.en: A spoken question mark. It makes a statement into a question
The shortcut question word which asks follow-up questions
The final particle which is added to sentences which already contain positive-negative-type questions or question words like mat1 je5
The particle made when ge3 is followed by aa3?
The question word which expects the listeners to be in agreement: that's right, isn't it?
The word which shows that things were different before but this is how the situation stands now
The word you use when you are trying to urge someone to do something for you or to persuade someone to agree with you
Makes a statement more emphatic: That's the way it is!
